title: Sorani Kurdish: A Language That Crossed Borders—and Refused to Be Defined by Them
deck: Across the mountains and cities of Iraq and Iran, Sorani Kurdish has carried generations of literature, memory, and everyday life. Its history is inseparable from the struggles of Kurdish communities for recognition, education, and cultural freedom—and from their determination to keep their language part of the future.

sections.heading: A Border Can Divide a People Without Dividing Their Language
sections.body:
Imagine speaking the same language as relatives living across a national border, yet growing up under entirely different rules about where that language belongs.

On one side, children may receive formal education through Kurdish. Public institutions, broadcasters, and publishers may use it as a language of administration, knowledge, and everyday communication.

On the other, speakers may face more limited opportunities to use Kurdish in formal education, even while it remains part of family life, literature, music, and community identity.

The language itself has not become less valuable when someone crosses the border.

What changes is the power of the institutions surrounding it.

This is one of the defining realities of **Sorani Kurdish**, also known as Central Kurdish and written as *کوردیی ناوەندی*.

Spoken primarily in parts of Iraq and Iran, and among communities living elsewhere in the world, Sorani is part of a wider Kurdish linguistic landscape whose history extends across several modern states.

It is a language of poetry, storytelling, education, journalism, conversation, and cultural expression.

Its speakers have maintained and developed a substantial written tradition while living through political upheaval, changing governments, migration, and, in some periods and places, devastating conflict and repression.

For Kurdish communities in Iraq, the twentieth century included some of the most brutal campaigns directed against a civilian population in the region's modern history.

Under Saddam Hussein's government, Kurdish areas experienced forced displacement, destruction of villages, mass killings, and chemical attacks.

The suffering was not merely a matter of whether Kurdish could be used in a classroom or government office. It involved the destruction of homes, communities, and human lives.

Yet the history of Sorani cannot be told only through suffering.

Across generations, Kurdish speakers continued writing, teaching, publishing, creating music, and raising children through their languages.

In Iraq, Kurdish later gained constitutional recognition as an official language alongside Arabic. Within the Kurdistan Region, Kurdish occupies a substantial place in education, public institutions, and cultural life.

Across the border in Iran, the legal, educational, and political circumstances are different.

And throughout the diaspora, speakers continue finding ways to maintain their language while adapting to life far from the places their families came from.

Sorani's story is therefore not one of disappearance followed by a simple return.

It is a story about the relationship between language and political power, the human consequences of repression and displacement, and the everyday work required to keep a language useful across generations.

**A border can determine which institutions recognize a language. It cannot determine the worth of the language—or the people who speak it.**

---

sections.heading: 01 — One Language, Different Political Worlds
sections.body:
### Understanding Sorani begins with understanding the diversity of Kurdish language and identity.

Kurdish is not a single, completely uniform spoken variety.

The Kurdish linguistic landscape includes several major varieties, among them Sorani, Kurmanji, and Southern Kurdish varieties, with differences in grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, and writing conventions.

Sorani, commonly called Central Kurdish, is especially associated with parts of northern Iraq and western Iran.

It belongs to the Iranian branch of the Indo-European language family and has developed an important modern written and literary tradition.

In much of its principal area of use, Sorani is written using a modified Arabic-based script adapted to Kurdish.

Its speakers use the language for everyday conversation, education, literature, broadcasting, journalism, and cultural expression.

But the institutions surrounding Sorani differ considerably depending on where its speakers live.

### Sorani in Iraq

In Iraq, Sorani has a prominent place in Kurdish cultural and institutional life, particularly in parts of the Kurdistan Region.

Cities such as Sulaymaniyah and Erbil have played important roles in Kurdish intellectual, educational, and political history, although the languages and varieties used within these cities and surrounding communities are not uniform.

Kurdish-language publishing, education, media, and public administration have developed through institutions shaped by Iraq's changing political circumstances.

The modern status of Kurdish in Iraq reflects decades of political struggle, periods of limited recognition, violent repression, and later constitutional change.

That history cannot be reduced to a straightforward progression from prohibition to freedom.

There were periods in which Kurdish-language cultural and educational activities existed alongside serious political restrictions and violence against Kurdish communities.

The recognition of Kurdish as an official language is therefore significant, but it must be understood within the broader history of the people whose rights and lives were affected.

### Sorani in Iran

Across the border in Iran, Sorani-speaking communities live under a different national legal and educational framework.

Persian is the dominant language of state administration and formal education.

Kurdish-speaking communities have maintained language use through families, literature, cultural activity, and other social settings, but access to Kurdish-language education and public institutions has not developed under the same arrangements as those in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.

Iran's constitutional framework makes provision for the use of regional and ethnic languages in press and mass media and for teaching their literature in schools alongside Persian. That provision should not be mistaken for a general guarantee of schooling through Sorani.

The gap between limited forms of recognition and the practical opportunities available to speakers remains important.

Political conditions, local practices, and opportunities for Kurdish cultural expression have also changed over time.

A truthful account should not present every Sorani-speaking community in Iran as experiencing identical restrictions.

Nor should it assume that developments in Iraq automatically apply across the border.

### Beyond Iraq and Iran

Migration and displacement have also created Kurdish-speaking communities in many other countries.

For diaspora families, maintaining Sorani can involve new challenges.

Children may grow up attending schools conducted in another national language. Parents may balance the demands of work, education, and integration with the desire to maintain Kurdish at home.

Community gatherings, cultural associations, language classes, digital media, and communication with relatives can help sustain connections.

But transmission is not guaranteed simply because a language remains important to family identity.

A child may understand Sorani without speaking it confidently.

Another may learn to read it through deliberate study rather than acquiring literacy through formal schooling.

The circumstances vary, but the underlying question is familiar:

**How can a language remain part of family life when the institutions surrounding its speakers operate primarily through another language?**

---

sections.heading: 02 — The History of Kurdish Communities Cannot Be Separated From Political Violence
sections.body:
### Language does not exist apart from the lives of its speakers.

It would be misleading to write about Kurdish language rights in Iraq without acknowledging the wider political history of Kurdish communities.

Throughout the twentieth century, Kurdish populations experienced conflict with successive governments, contested political arrangements, forced migration, and periods of severe repression.

The degree and form of that repression varied between countries, governments, regions, and historical periods.

For Kurdish civilians in Iraq under Saddam Hussein, the consequences became catastrophic.

### The Anfal Campaign and the Destruction of Communities

During the late 1980s, the Iraqi government conducted the Anfal campaign against Kurdish areas.

The campaign involved mass killings, forced displacement, destruction of villages, and other grave abuses.

In March 1988, Iraqi government forces carried out a chemical attack on Halabja, killing thousands of civilians and injuring many others. Halabja is closely associated with Sorani-speaking Kurdish society, but the wider Anfal campaign affected Kurdish communities beyond a single linguistic variety.

The scale of suffering must not be reduced to a metaphor about language loss.

People were killed.

Families were displaced.

Homes and villages were destroyed.

Survivors carried the consequences of violence into the years that followed.

For communities whose languages are sustained through family relationships, local institutions, and everyday interaction, such destruction can also damage the social environments through which knowledge and language are passed on.

But it is important to distinguish that consequence from the principal nature of the violence.

The Anfal campaign was a campaign of mass repression against Kurdish populations. It should not be inaccurately described as merely a government program to prohibit Sorani vocabulary or writing.

The suffering of Kurdish civilians deserves to be acknowledged in its own right.

### What Displacement Means for a Living Language

When a community experiences forced displacement, the damage extends beyond the loss of physical homes.

Families may be separated.

Children may grow up far from relatives and community networks.

Schools, libraries, cultural institutions, and ordinary gathering places may be lost or disrupted.

People who once shared a language in daily life may find themselves scattered across different cities or countries.

Such conditions can make language transmission more difficult.

They can also generate new forms of community organization, as displaced people work to maintain cultural relationships in unfamiliar places.

But no account of resilience should imply that the suffering was necessary or beneficial.

Kurdish literature, education, and cultural expression did not become meaningful because communities suffered.

They were meaningful before the violence, remained meaningful during it, and continue to matter afterward.

**The destruction of a community is not simply a chapter in the history of its language. It is a human catastrophe whose effects can reach into every part of community life.**

Acknowledging that history gives proper weight to the rights and institutions Kurdish speakers have struggled to secure.

---

sections.heading: 03 — The Language That Continued to Be Written
sections.body:
### Sorani's story is also a history of literature, scholarship, and cultural creation.

Sorani possesses a substantial modern written tradition.

Its development as a literary language reflects the work of poets, scholars, writers, publishers, educators, and generations of readers.

Kurdish literary history is diverse, extending across multiple varieties and regions, but Sorani occupies an important place within that broader tradition.

One significant historical figure is the nineteenth-century Kurdish poet Nali, whose work is associated with the development of Sorani as a major literary language.

Later writers and intellectuals continued to expand Kurdish literary expression through poetry, prose, journalism, scholarship, and education.

These achievements matter because they challenge an incomplete view of language preservation.

Sorani was not simply a spoken language waiting for modern institutions to give it a written form.

It had already developed traditions of literary and intellectual expression.

### Why Written Culture Matters

A written language allows knowledge and expression to travel beyond an immediate conversation.

A poem can reach readers who never met its author.

A newspaper can create a shared space for public discussion.

A textbook can help students encounter complex subjects through a language they understand.

A dictionary can support learners, writers, and educators in developing accuracy and consistency.

For Sorani, literature and publishing have helped sustain the language's role in intellectual and public life.

But writing should not be treated as the only measure of a language's value.

The spoken relationships through which children acquire language remain just as important.

A language can possess a sophisticated literary tradition and still face difficulties in education or family transmission under particular political and social conditions.

Likewise, a strong public-language framework does not eliminate the need for communities to sustain everyday use.

### Culture Is More Than Survival

Kurdish poetry, music, storytelling, and cultural traditions should not be described only as evidence that people resisted oppression.

They are also forms of artistic and intellectual achievement in their own right.

Writers create because they have something to say.

Musicians perform because their communities have histories of sound, expression, and celebration.

Families tell stories because those stories belong to their relationships and experiences.

When every cultural achievement is presented solely as a response to persecution, the people involved risk being reduced to the suffering imposed upon them.

Sorani-speaking communities have histories far richer than the restrictions they have endured.

They have created literature, scholarship, humor, entertainment, education, and public debate.

Their language is a means of expressing ordinary and extraordinary human experience.

**Sorani is not valuable only because it has survived difficult history. It is valuable because it continues to carry the lives, knowledge, and creativity of the people who use it.**

---

sections.heading: 04 — Official Recognition and the Right to Use Kurdish
sections.body:
### Legal status can transform what becomes possible in public life.

In 2005, Iraq adopted a Constitution establishing Arabic and Kurdish as the country's official languages.

Article 4 is a major legal milestone.

It recognizes Kurdish at the national level and addresses the use of official languages in education and public communication, alongside provisions concerning other language communities.

For Kurdish speakers, this recognition represents an important change in the legal position of the language.

But the Constitution refers to **Kurdish broadly**, not exclusively to Sorani.

That distinction matters.

Different Kurdish varieties are used in different parts of Iraq, and national recognition should not be presented as a law concerned only with one of them.

### Recognition Does Not Automatically Create Equal Access

A constitutional right can establish important obligations.

But it does not guarantee that every person can use their language equally in every setting.

Public services need appropriate systems and staff.

Schools need teachers and educational materials.

Official documents require accurate language support.

Broadcasting, publishing, and administrative institutions need resources.

Implementation also varies across regions and public bodies.

For that reason, the existence of official recognition should be understood as a significant achievement rather than evidence that every practical challenge has been resolved.

The same distinction applies to language use across borders.

Iraq's constitutional protections cannot be treated as rights automatically available to Kurdish speakers in Iran.

A legal framework belongs to the jurisdiction that established it.

### The Kurdistan Region's Public-Language Framework

The Kurdistan Region of Iraq has also developed regional policies supporting Kurdish in public life.

The Kurdistan Region's Official Languages Law of 2014 forms part of that framework.

In February 2023, the Kurdistan Regional Government announced measures concerning Kurdish-language learning for foreign residents and the use of Kurdish in signage, menus, guidance, and public instructions.

These announcements illustrate an important aspect of language policy.

A language needs practical opportunities for use.

It matters whether someone can read a public notice, obtain information, understand instructions, or communicate in a public setting through the language.

Such opportunities may seem ordinary.

That is precisely their significance.

A language becomes securely embedded in public life when it can be used for ordinary tasks—not only cultural celebrations or official ceremonies.

The 2023 announcements describe government policy intentions and directives. They should not be taken as independent evidence that every measure has been fully implemented.

The work of implementation matters as much as the announcement.

**A language's public standing is measured not only by what a law permits, but by what people can actually do through it.**

---

sections.heading: 05 — A Living Language Needs Everyday Opportunities
sections.body:
### Sorani's future cannot be measured by legal recognition alone.

In parts of Iraqi Kurdistan, Sorani occupies a substantial place in education, publishing, broadcasting, and administration.

These are meaningful institutional foundations.

They allow speakers to encounter Kurdish as a language of contemporary knowledge and public participation.

But the conditions of daily language use are not identical across all Kurdish communities.

In Iran, the dominance of Persian in state education creates different circumstances.

In diaspora settings, children may grow up with limited access to formal Sorani instruction.

Even where schooling and media are available, patterns of family language transmission can change over time.

The task is therefore not simply to increase the visibility of Sorani.

It is to sustain the conditions in which people can use it naturally.

### Education Is More Than Vocabulary

When children receive education through a language, they encounter it as a means of understanding the world.

They can use it to learn mathematics, history, science, literature, and other subjects.

They can ask questions and express complex ideas.

That is different from studying a language for a limited number of hours each week.

Both forms of learning can have value, but they provide different opportunities.

For Sorani, the availability of Kurdish-medium education in parts of Iraq represents an important institutional resource.

Where comparable pathways are limited, families and learners may rely more heavily on community teaching, private study, digital materials, and cultural organizations.

Those differences should be recognized rather than concealed under a single claim that Kurdish education is either universally available or universally prohibited.

### The Importance of Family and Community

Language transmission is ultimately a human activity.

Children develop confidence through listening, responding, asking questions, and interacting with others.

Families create some of the earliest opportunities for those experiences.

Community institutions can extend them.

Writers, teachers, broadcasters, and digital creators help provide material through which a language continues developing.

Diaspora communities may use online communication, cultural events, and educational resources to maintain connections across distance.

But access to resources does not automatically create fluent speakers.

A dictionary cannot replace conversation.

A legal right cannot ensure that every family uses the language at home.

A school cannot guarantee that its graduates will have opportunities to use Sorani throughout adulthood.

These limitations do not diminish the achievements already made.

They clarify what continued support requires.

### The Future Must Belong to Contemporary Speakers

Sorani is not simply an inheritance to be preserved unchanged.

Its speakers continue developing vocabulary, producing literature, creating media, and communicating about modern life.

The language is used to discuss technology, relationships, education, politics, work, and the experiences of younger generations.

These activities matter because a living language must be able to express the present.

Young speakers should not have to choose between participation in contemporary society and continued use of their language.

The strongest future for Sorani is one in which it remains a practical, expressive, and valued means of communication across the environments where its speakers live.

---

sections.heading: 06 — Making Room for Sorani in the Digital World
sections.body:
### A language's writing system deserves technical accuracy as well as cultural respect.

Sorani is commonly written in a modified Arabic-based script, read from right to left.

Its written conventions include characters that may be unfamiliar to people who ordinarily type in English, Arabic, or Persian.

These distinctions matter.

Some characters used in Kurdish writing resemble characters in other scripts but have different underlying Unicode code points.

Other letters are specific to the orthographic needs of Kurdish.

For accurate Sorani practice, it is important to use an appropriate keyboard and preserve the intended characters.

### Why the Correct Characters Matter

Examples of Sorani characters that deserve careful attention include:

**ڕ ڵ ۆ ێ ە**

These are not decorative alternatives to Latin letters or automatically interchangeable with similar-looking Arabic or Persian forms.

Replacing a character may change the written word or cause a text-comparison system to identify a mismatch.

For learners, the problem can be especially confusing when two characters look nearly identical on screen but are represented differently in the underlying text.

A responsible typing activity should therefore support accurate input rather than encouraging users to substitute whichever character is easiest to enter.

### Right-to-Left Writing Requires Care

The direction of Sorani writing creates technical considerations for a typing-test website.

Text must display correctly from right to left.

Cursor movement, punctuation placement, selection behavior, and the interaction of Kurdish text with numbers or Latin characters all require testing.

Unicode normalization and input methods also matter when comparing the typed result with a source passage.

A mismatch should not automatically be interpreted as a learner's failure to understand the language.

It may result from keyboard configuration, character substitution, text processing, or input composition.

For that reason, technical compatibility should be checked before new material is introduced as a scored typing exercise.

### Accuracy Before Speed

Begin with short, reliable source material.

Use an appropriate Kurdish keyboard.

Read the passage before starting and check unfamiliar vocabulary through trusted learning resources.

Preserve spelling, punctuation, and the intended characters.

If a character cannot be entered correctly, resolve the input-method problem before measuring speed.

For Sorani, as for every language in this series, a standard five-character words-per-minute calculation is a mechanical measurement.

It does not measure fluency.

It does not establish cultural knowledge.

And it cannot meaningfully compare the linguistic difficulty of unrelated writing systems.

**A language deserves to be represented accurately before anyone attempts to type it quickly.**

---

sections.heading: 07 — Why WPMTest Includes Sorani Kurdish
sections.body:
### A keyboard can introduce a language. It cannot tell the whole story of its people.

The Living Languages Series explores the relationship between language, political power, education, community continuity, and efforts to strengthen everyday use.

Sorani belongs in this collection because its history reveals how dramatically the position of a language can change across political borders.

It also demonstrates why linguistic rights cannot be discussed separately from the circumstances of the people who speak the language.

For Kurdish communities, language is one part of a wider history involving literature, public institutions, political struggles, displacement, cultural achievement, and continuing community life.

WPMTest does not claim to represent these communities or speak on their behalf.

Nor can a typing exercise repair historical injustice, replace language education, or resolve differences in public-language rights.

Our contribution is deliberately limited.

We can provide an introductory historical account, encourage accurate engagement with Sorani's writing system, and direct attention toward resources created by people with relevant linguistic and community knowledge.

The current introductory Sorani pathway provides character and language-name copying exercises, alongside the option to use text whose language, spelling, and usage rights have been independently verified.

It does not yet claim to offer a speaker-reviewed collection of complete Sorani sentences.

Before new scored passages are published, they should receive competent language review and technical testing for right-to-left display and input behavior.

The goal is not to make a claim about saving the language.

It is to approach the language with respect and recognize the people who continue sustaining it.

**Sorani's value is not determined by the borders its speakers cross, the institutions that recognize it, or the speed at which its words can be typed.**

Its value lives in the people who speak, write, teach, and create through it.

---

sections.heading: Turning Points in Sorani Kurdish's Story
sections.body:
**Nineteenth Century — The Development of Modern Sorani Literature**

Poets including Nali contribute to the development of Sorani as an important literary language, building on wider Kurdish traditions of poetry and scholarship.

**Twentieth Century — Literature, Education, and Political Change**

Sorani continues developing as a language of publishing, education, and public expression while Kurdish communities experience changing political conditions across Iraq and Iran.

**1988 — Anfal and Halabja**

During the Anfal campaign, the Iraqi government carries out mass repression against Kurdish populations. A chemical attack on Halabja kills thousands of civilians. These events form part of the broader history of violence against Kurdish communities, not a prohibition specific to Sorani.

**2005 — Kurdish Gains Constitutional Recognition in Iraq**

Article 4 of Iraq's Constitution establishes Kurdish and Arabic as official languages, providing a major legal milestone for Kurdish-language rights.

**2014 — A Regional Official-Languages Framework**

The Kurdistan Region's Official Languages Law provides a framework concerning the use of languages in regional public life.

**2023 — Measures for Kurdish in Everyday Public Settings**

The Kurdistan Regional Government announces measures concerning Kurdish-language learning for foreign residents and the use of Kurdish in public signage, menus, guidance, and instructions.

**Today — A Language Across Borders and Generations**

Sorani continues through education, publishing, broadcasting, family life, cultural activity, and digital communication in Iraq, Iran, and diaspora communities.

*These are selected historical milestones, not a complete history. Different Kurdish communities and language varieties have experienced distinct political conditions. Legal recognition in Iraq does not establish equivalent rights in Iran or other countries.*

---

sections.body:

Listening helps learners encounter pronunciation, rhythm, vocabulary, and natural patterns of speech.

Structured learning resources can complement reading and typing, particularly when they provide authentic audio and clearly identify the Kurdish variety being taught.

sections.heading: A Language That Belongs to More Than One Side of a Border
sections.body:
There is a powerful truth at the heart of Sorani's story.

A language can belong to people whose lives are governed by different countries, different laws, and different political histories.

One community may have access to education through the language.

Another may maintain it primarily through families, literature, cultural activity, and community teaching.

Some speakers live close to the places where generations of relatives have lived.

Others have been separated from those places by migration, displacement, or conflict.

The circumstances change.

The importance of the language does not.

Sorani's history includes profound suffering.

The violence experienced by Kurdish civilians in Iraq, including the Anfal campaign and the chemical attack on Halabja, cannot be softened into abstract language about political difficulty.

People lost their homes, relatives, communities, and lives.

Those losses deserve remembrance without exaggeration and without turning them into a convenient dramatic backdrop.

But Kurdish history is also a history of intellectual achievement, literature, teaching, music, cultural expression, and ordinary human relationships.

Sorani speakers have continued writing, creating, educating children, and participating in public life through their language.

In Iraq, constitutional recognition and Kurdish-language institutions have expanded important opportunities for use.

In Iran, Sorani-speaking communities continue maintaining their language under a different legal and educational system.

Across the diaspora, families and cultural organizations work to preserve connections that geography can make difficult to sustain.

None of these achievements erases the past.

Nor do they guarantee that every speaker will have equal opportunities in the future.

There remains work to be done in education, community language use, digital accessibility, cultural support, and the practical implementation of linguistic rights.

Yet the existence of that unfinished work is not a reason to dismiss what has already been achieved.

Sorani is not a language that exists only because it has survived repression.

It is a language through which people continue living.

It carries the voices of writers and teachers, parents and grandparents, students and young creators.

It is heard in conversation, used in education, written in books, shared through media, and carried between communities separated by distance.

Its future will not be determined by one law, one government, or one institution.

It will continue to be shaped by the people who use it.

**Borders may divide the places where Sorani is spoken. They do not erase the relationships, knowledge, and cultural life carried through the language.**

And wherever a new generation has the opportunity to learn, speak, and create through Sorani, another part of that future remains possible.

**Sorani Kurdish is not simply a language that endured history. It is a living language whose speakers continue writing what comes next.**

---

sections.heading: Sources, Photography, and Editorial Care
sections.body:
The central historical and institutional account draws on the following references:

1. [The Cambridge History of the Kurds (2021)](https://www.cambridge.org/9781108473354) — Scholarly historical context concerning Kurdish societies, language varieties, literature, and political developments.

2. [Iraq Constitution — Article 4](https://presidency.gov.krd/krp/uploadedforms/IraqConstitutionA.pdf) — Constitutional recognition of Arabic and Kurdish as official languages in Iraq.

3. [Kurdistan Regional Government — Mother Language Day Decrees, February 2023](https://gov.krd/english/government/the-prime-minister/activities/posts/2023/february/prime-minister-barzani-issues-two-decrees-on-international-mother-tongue-language-day/) — Official announcements concerning Kurdish-language learning and public communication.

**Additional sources required for the expanded historical account**

Before publication, add direct scholarly or institutional references concerning:

- The Anfal campaign and the March 1988 chemical attack on Halabja, preferably from recognized historical research or human-rights documentation.
- The development of Sorani literary traditions, including the work of Nali.
- Iran's constitutional provisions concerning regional and ethnic languages, and credible research on Kurdish-language educational access.
- The Kurdistan Region's 2014 Official Languages Law and the specific provisions relevant to Kurdish.

These subjects expand beyond the three sources in the original article and should receive dedicated citations.

### Photography

Lake Dukan, Sulaymaniyah Governorate, Kurdistan Region of Iraq.

Photograph: [Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:7._Lake_Dukan,_Sulaymaniyah_Governorate,_Iraqi_Kurdistan.jpg) · [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0).

This photograph introduces one part of the region associated with Sorani-speaking communities. It does not represent the experiences of all Kurdish speakers in Iraq, Iran, or the diaspora.

### Our Editorial Approach

This article distinguishes Sorani from other Kurdish language varieties and avoids applying restrictions documented in one country or linguistic community to all Kurdish speakers.

Iraq's constitutional recognition of Kurdish is described as recognition of Kurdish broadly, not Sorani alone.

Historical violence against Kurdish civilians is discussed as part of the wider experience of Kurdish communities and is not misrepresented as a language-specific prohibition.

Legal recognition, government announcements, and policy objectives are not treated as independent evidence that every promised measure has been fully implemented.

This is a source-based editorial account, not a claim of fluent-speaker or specialist endorsement. Newly developed Sorani sentence passages require appropriate linguistic review and right-to-left technical testing before publication.

[Send a Correction or Offer Language Review →](https://wpmtest.app/contact/)
